_meta.source: LINDDUN PRO Privacy Threat Modeling Tutorial v0.1 (April 2023) and the official LINDDUN threat type catalog (linddun.org/threat-types, linddun.org/linddun-go-categories)
_meta.citation: Laurens Sion and Wouter Joosen, LINDDUN PRO privacy threat modeling tutorial, Technical Report, KU Leuven, April 2023
_meta.note: L, Dd, and D nodes are transcribed verbatim from the printed trees in the v0.1 tutorial. I, Nr, U, and Nc nodes are reconstructed from the official LINDDUN threat-type catalog (the v0.1 tutorial summarizes these four via type definitions only). The official trees expand each type into characteristics; the structure here follows the published sub-characteristics. IMPORTANT: gold-standard threats (e.g. KidsTube HW2) may cite instance-specific sub-IDs (e.g. Dd.4.5, L.1.3, Nc.1.2) that extend an official node with a project-local numbering. Such IDs denote 'another instance of the parent official node', not a different official node. Verify against the latest full trees at https://downloads.linddun.org before publication.
_meta.id_convention: Dotted IDs follow the official notation where available. A gold-standard ID like Dd.4.5 should be read as an instance under the official Dd.4 (Involved parties and exposure) family.

L.name: Linking
L.definition: Associating data items or actions to learn more about an individual or group. Linking relies on a recurring identifier, a combination of attributes (quasi-identifiers), or a profile that allows data to be singled out. Linking becomes problematic when it enables inference, singling out, or profiling.

L.1.1.title: Unique identifier
L.1.1.description: Linking based on an identifier that is unique (globally or locally, within the system or across the context boundary).

L.2.title: Linkable data
L.2.description: Linking through the combination or analysis of data.

L.2.1.1.title: Quasi-identifier combining data of a single individual
L.2.1.1.description: Linking through a set of attributes that can serve as a quasi-identifier.

L.2.1.2.title: Combining data of different individuals
L.2.1.2.description: Linking through combining data of different individuals.

L.2.2.1.title: Profiling an individual
L.2.2.1.description: Personal data of an individual is analyzed for patterns to link data to that individual, based on the data or user actions.

L.2.2.2.title: Profiling a group of individuals
L.2.2.2.description: Data of a single individual leads to insights about a larger group; knowledge transfers through known relations of group membership or similarity.

L.2.2.3.title: Profiling an individual through (dis)similarity
L.2.2.3.description: Applying methods to assess uniqueness or similarity to predict relevant properties.

I.name: Identifying
I.definition: Learning the identity of an individual. Identifying threats arise when identity can be revealed through leaks, deduction, or inference when this is unintentional or undesired. Identifying is related to linking and can lead to unawareness and non-compliance issues.

I.1.title: Identified data
I.1.description: The system explicitly maintains or refers to the link to the identity (e.g. in content or metadata). Identity is directly revealed through identifying data such as name, government ID, or email.

I.1.1.title: Identifying through explicit identifier
I.1.1.description: An explicit identifier (real name, government ID, account email) directly reveals the data subject's identity when collected, transmitted, or stored.

I.1.2.title: Identifying through credential or identity reuse
I.1.2.description: Reuse of an identity-bearing credential (e.g. shared login, reused email) ties an action or record to an identified individual.

I.2.title: Identifiable data
I.2.description: Identity can be derived indirectly, e.g. from pseudonyms, identity-revealing content, a small anonymity set, or metadata.

I.2.1.title: Identifying through identity-revealing content or metadata
I.2.1.description: Identity is inferred from content or metadata (e.g. tokens, payloads, document metadata) that reveals who is involved.

I.2.2.title: Identifying through small anonymity set or weak verification
I.2.2.description: Identity is deduced because the set of candidates is small, or because a weak verification mechanism fails to protect the identity boundary.

Nr.name: Non-repudiation
Nr.definition: An individual is unable to deny a claim (knowing, having done, having said something) because the system retains attributable evidence. Two dimensions: (i) the strength of the evidence regarding the claim, and (ii) the strength of attributability to an individual. In privacy, non-repudiation is a threat (loss of plausible deniability), the inverse of its security-goal role.

Nr.1.title: Retained evidence of a claim/action
Nr.1.description: The system retains evidence regarding a particular action or fact (log files, digital signatures, document metadata, watermarked data, persistent identifiers) that impacts deniability.

Nr.1.1.title: Attributable persistent logging
Nr.1.1.description: Actions are logged with timestamps and attributable identifiers, creating an irrefutable record the individual cannot deny.

Nr.1.2.title: Irrevocable attributed content
Nr.1.2.description: Content authored by the individual (e.g. comments, submissions) is stored with attribution and cannot be removed, permanently preventing deniability.

D.name: Detecting
D.definition: Becoming aware of data-subject involvement, membership, or participation by observing the existence of relevant information. Detecting does NOT require access to the data itself; observing existence, side-effects, or communication flows can be sufficient.

D.1.title: Observed communications
D.1.description: Detecting through observed communications. An adversary observing requests/flows can detect involvement even when content is encrypted.

D.1.1.title: Network-observable actions
D.1.1.description: Requests and actions are observable on the network (e.g. unencrypted or pattern-revealing traffic), allowing an observer to detect a subject's activity.

D.2.title: Application side-effect
D.2.description: Detecting through (trans)action side-effects (e.g. temporary files in the file system, URL preview fetches, scanners triggering requests).

D.3.title: System responses
D.3.description: The existence of an item of interest is revealed in a system response, evoked deliberately (probing) or given accidentally.

Dd.name: Data Disclosure
Dd.definition: Cases in which explicit (intended/designed) or implicit (unintended/consequential) disclosure of personal data across a boundary is avoidable. The minimality principle is key: only collect, process, store, and share strictly required personal data.

Dd.1.title: Unnecessary data types
Dd.1.description: Data can be highly sensitive depending on context and should only be collected/processed when strictly required.

Dd.1.1.title: Data type sensitivity
Dd.1.1.description: More sensitive data types are collected than functionally required by the system.

Dd.1.2.title: Data type granularity
Dd.1.2.description: Disclosed personal data is of a more fine-grained level of granularity than needed.

Dd.1.3.title: Data type encoding
Dd.1.3.description: The encoding of the data includes additional personal data that is not functionally needed (e.g. an ID image embedding far more than an age).

Dd.2.title: Excessive volume
Dd.2.description: Concerns the volume of personal data collected and processed.

Dd.2.1.title: Amount
Dd.2.1.description: An excessive amount of personal data is processed beyond what is functionally needed.

Dd.2.2.title: Frequency
Dd.2.2.description: Personal data is processed more frequently than functionally needed.

Dd.2.3.title: Involved data subjects
Dd.2.3.description: Personal data is processed of more data subjects than functionally needed.

Dd.3.title: Unnecessary processing
Dd.3.description: Whether the processing and treatment of personal data is actually necessary for the functional goals.

Dd.3.1.title: Treatment, analysis, enrichment, transformation
Dd.3.1.description: Personal data is further treated, analyzed, and enriched in a way not necessary to achieve the functionality.

Dd.3.2.title: Propagation
Dd.3.2.description: Data is accessible by or propagated to other services where it is not needed.

Dd.3.3.title: Implicit data disclosure
Dd.3.3.description: Data is implicitly collected as a side-effect of explicit data disclosures or data flows (e.g. unencrypted transmission exposing data to network observers).

Dd.3.4.title: Duration/retention
Dd.3.4.description: Personal data is processed or kept longer than functionally needed.

Dd.4.title: Involved parties and exposure
Dd.4.description: Distinction between exposure to known/anticipated external parties versus data published or broadcast broadly (which amplifies risk). Also covers insecure exposure of stored data.

Dd.4.1.title: Involved parties
Dd.4.1.description: Personal data made accessible to more parties than functionally necessary.

Dd.4.1.1.title: Predetermined set of parties
Dd.4.1.1.description: Parties with whom data is shared are known up front; the set is static and fixed.

Dd.4.1.2.title: Dynamic set of parties
Dd.4.1.2.description: Parties with whom data is shared are determined dynamically and may change frequently.

Dd.4.2.title: Availability/accessibility of data
Dd.4.2.description: Personal data is published or made accessible more broadly than necessary (e.g. insecure storage, broad access).

U.name: Unawareness and unintervenability
U.definition: Lack of support offered to involved/affected individuals: insufficiently informing, involving, or empowering the data subject. Three potential lacks: (i) transparency, (ii) user feedback/awareness of impact, and (iii) intervenability (controls to influence data handling).

U.1.title: Lack of transparency / awareness
U.1.description: Not properly informing data subjects about data collection and what happens with that data; users unaware of collection or impact.

U.1.1.title: No notice of data collection
U.1.1.description: Data subjects are not informed that their data is collected or processed (e.g. silent tracking with no notice).

U.1.2.title: Covert processing / surveillance without transparency
U.1.2.description: Data is processed or disclosed to others (e.g. surveillance, profiling) without age-appropriate or adequate transparency to the data subject.

U.1.3.title: Undisclosed granularity or purpose
U.1.3.description: The detail, granularity, or purpose of collection is not disclosed (e.g. fine-grained behavioral tracking not stated in the policy).

U.2.title: Lack of intervenability / control
U.2.description: Not providing data subjects with the controls or means to influence how their data is handled (access, correction, deletion).

U.2.1.title: Insufficient or contradicted controls
U.2.1.description: Promised controls (e.g. deletion) are absent, incomplete, or contradicted by actual data persistence.

Nc.name: Non-compliance
Nc.definition: Lack of adherence to legislation, regulation, standards, and best practices, leading to incomplete management of risk. Focuses on the intersection between identified privacy threats and broader risk notions (legal, cybersecurity, organizational). Covers unlawful processing, lack of data lifecycle management, and lack of security hardening.

Nc.1.title: Compliance-related problem
Nc.1.description: A compliance problem deriving from applicable L/I/Nr/D/Dd/U threats, translated into legal/regulatory risk (GDPR, COPPA, CCPA, etc.).

Nc.1.1.title: Unlawful processing or disclosure
Nc.1.1.description: Processing or disclosure of personal data without a lawful basis or required consent (e.g. sharing children's data without verifiable parental consent).

Nc.1.2.title: Violation of data-protection principle
Nc.1.2.description: Systematic violation of a core principle such as data minimization, purpose limitation, or storage limitation across the system.

Nc.1.3.title: Inadequate consent or safeguard mechanism
Nc.1.3.description: A required consent, verification, or safeguard mechanism is missing or inadequate to meet the applicable regulation (e.g. no FTC-approved verifiable parental consent method).
